summary: A Best Current Practice with examples of Session Initiation Protocol services, covering most features of IP Centrex and PBX offerings. Most services are done in SIP user agents, although some need a SIP proxy or extensions such as REFER, SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY. It gives examples of call flows for these features.

eli5.summary: Office phones can transfer calls, hold them, or forward them. This shows with step-by-step examples how to do the same things using internet phone messages.

questions: how does sip attended transfer work
how does sip call hold work
subtitle: Worked SIP call flows for 18 classic office-phone features, from call hold to click to dial.

tldr.problem: Businesses expect IP phones to offer the features of a PBX or an IP Centrex service, such as hold, transfer, forwarding and call pickup, but SIP itself only defines the building blocks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through 18 services message by message, showing which SIP methods, header fields and extensions (REFER, Replaces, Join, SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY) a phone or proxy uses to deliver each one.
tldr.outcome: It is a companion to the SIP specifications, not a protocol: it shows one working way to do each service, and says other approaches such as 3pcc or B2BUAs are not excluded.

today: RFC 5359 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 144) published in October 2008. The unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it, and its examples are meant to be read alongside the SIP specifications, which remain definitive for protocol questions.

sections.title: What the Document Covers
sections.content:
RFC 5359 gives example call flows for a SIP implementation of traditional telephony services. It lists 18: call hold, consultation hold, music on hold, unattended transfer, attended transfer, instant messaging transfer, unconditional call forwarding, forwarding on busy, forwarding on no answer, two kinds of 3-way conference, find-me, incoming and outgoing call screening, call park, call pickup, automatic redial and click to dial.

The flows came out of the design of a SIP IP communications network and stand for so-called IP Centrex or PBX services. They are meant as a companion to RFC 3261 (SIP 2.0) and its extensions, with session descriptions following RFC 3264, and they assume the basic behavior explored in RFC 3665.

The RFC is explicit that the SIP specifications are definitive on protocol questions, and that these are not the only ways to build the services. Third Party Call Control (RFC 3725) or Back-to-Back User Agents are also possible.
sections.eli5: Think of a recipe book for phone tricks. It shows 18 tricks, like putting someone on hold, and lists exactly which messages to send for each. It says there may be other recipes that work too.

sections.title: Building Blocks and Conventions
sections.content:
Most services are done in the SIP user agents, with a proxy helping in some. Several rely on extensions: the REFER method (RFC 3515), the Replaces header field (RFC 3891), the Join header field (RFC 3911), and SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY from RFC 3265. The dialog event package is in RFC 4235, and some examples use GRUU addresses so a user agent can be reached outside its existing dialog.

The flows use secure SIP URIs (sips), implying TLS on each hop with assumed certificate validation, and show Digest authentication in some examples. Only simple audio SDP offer/answer exchanges appear, and the flows apply equally to other media.

Each flow comes with a description, a message flow diagram and the detailed content of every message. Messages are labeled F1, F2 and so on. In the diagrams, dashed lines (---) are mandatory control messages, double dashes (===) are media paths, and messages in parentheses are optional. For readability the examples simplify things: Digest responses are not real MD5 values, Call-IDs are often reused, CSeq often starts at 1, and content lengths are shown as ....
sections.eli5: The phones already know how to call each other. This section lists the extra tools they borrow for the fancy tricks, and explains the drawing style, like which line means a message and which means voice.

sections.title: Holding a Call and Music on Hold
sections.content:
In the call hold flow, Alice calls Bob and Bob puts the call on hold, then takes it off hold before Alice hangs up. Hold is unidirectional in nature, but a user agent that puts the other party on hold will generally also stop sending media. Older user agents set the connection address to 0.0.0.0; that behavior is deprecated in favor of the a=inactive SDP attribute if no media is sent, or a=sendonly if media is still sent. The re-INVITE also carries the rendering feature tag from RFC 4235 to show that Bob's phone is no longer rendering media to Bob.

Consultation hold extends this: Bob holds Alice, calls Carol, disconnects from Carol and then takes Alice off hold.

For music on hold, Bob sends a REFER to a Music Server, which sends an INVITE with Replaces to Alice and then plays RTP music to her. Bob resumes by sending an INVITE with Replaces to Alice. The server advertises itself with the automaton and byeless feature tags. If Alice does not want music, her phone can refuse the INVITE and she stays on hold in silence.
sections.eli5: Holding a call is like saying 'one moment' and covering the phone. Music on hold is like handing the caller to a friend who plays a record until you come back.

sections.title: Call Transfer
sections.content:
In the unattended transfer, Bob calls Alice and Alice transfers Bob to Carol by sending a REFER with a Refer-To of Carol. Bob sets up the session to Carol and reports success back in a NOTIFY. If the transfer fails, Bob can send a new INVITE to Alice to re-establish the session. Despite the BYE Alice sends, the dialog between Alice and Bob still exists until the subscription created by the REFER ends, through a NOTIFY with Subscription-State: terminated;reason=noresource or a 481 response to a NOTIFY.

In the attended transfer, Alice calls Bob, Bob holds Alice and calls Carol to announce the transfer, then holds Carol. Bob transfers Alice to Carol, and the new session replaces the one between Bob and Carol. Bob inserts a Replaces header field into the Refer-To URI, using the Contact URI Carol returned in her 200 OK, so only the correct instance of Carol is reached. A gr URI parameter shows that Contact is a GRUU.

In the instant messaging transfer, Bob sends Carol a SIP MESSAGE containing Alice's URI with an embedded Replaces header field. If Carol clicks the URI, her phone sends an INVITE to Alice that replaces the session with Bob. Another IM protocol could carry the URI instead.
sections.eli5: An unattended transfer is like passing a phone to a coworker without checking they are free. An attended transfer is like first asking the coworker, and then handing it over. The IM version is like texting the coworker a link to take over the call.

sections.title: Forwarding and Find-Me
sections.content:
In unconditional forwarding, Bob wants all calls sent to the PSTN, which is just another URI to the proxy. When Alice calls Bob, the proxy rewrites the Request URI and forwards the INVITE to a Gateway. The 181 Call is Being Forwarded response is shown as sent by the proxy, though strictly the proxy is behaving as a user agent, since a proxy cannot generate non-100 provisional responses. Forwarding could also be done with a 302 Moved Temporarily redirect.

In forwarding on busy, calls to B1 go to B2 if B1 is busy, information the proxy knows. In forwarding on no answer, the proxy places the call to B2 if nobody answers B1.

Find-me tries to locate Bob by calling locations from a list of contacts. The location that answers becomes the active set, and no other sets may join the call. The flow shows a sequential search, but parallel forking could be used.
sections.eli5: Forwarding is like a note on your door saying 'if I am not here, try next door'. Find-me is a receptionist who tries your desk, then your cell phone, until someone picks up.

sections.title: Three-Way Conferences
sections.content:
There are two flows. In third party is added, Alice and Bob are in a 2-party call and Bob wants to add Carol. Bob can mix media, so he first sends Alice a re-INVITE that changes his Contact URI to one indicating his mixer, and includes the isfocus feature tag as described in RFC 4579. He then INVITEs Carol using the same Contact URI. Bob could wait to re-INVITE Alice until Carol has answered, and could put Alice on hold before calling Carol.

In third party joins, Carol wants to join the existing call. She may have learned the dialog identifier by non-SIP means or from a dialog-package NOTIFY sent by Bob. She sends Bob an INVITE with a Join header field identifying the Alice-Bob dialog. Bob re-INVITEs Alice to switch to focus mode, with the isfocus tag, then accepts Carol's INVITE, producing the 3-way call.
sections.eli5: Bob is the host of a call and has a way to mix voices. Either he invites Carol in, or Carol asks to join, and then all three can talk at once.

sections.title: Call Screening
sections.content:
In incoming call screening, Bob has a list of addresses from which he will not accept calls, and Alice is on it. Bob does not accept INVITEs that have not been screened by the proxy. Screening cannot be done using the From header; some form of authentication credentials must be used. The screening proxy rejects Alice's call and inserts an announcement URI in an Error-Info header field, which Alice can access by sending an INVITE to listen to the announcement. The Announcement Server uses the automaton and rendering feature tags to show it is a media server only able to play announcements.

In outgoing call screening, Alice has a list of addresses she cannot call, and Bob is on it. When she tries to call Bob, she can again set up a session to hear the announcement in the Error-Info header field.
sections.eli5: It is like a bouncer with a list. If your name is on the blocked list, the call is turned away, and you may get a recorded message explaining why.

sections.title: Park, Pickup, Redial and Click to Dial
sections.content:
Call park is a special case of transfer. Bob sends a REFER to a Park Server, which sends Alice an INVITE with Replaces. Alice accepts and sends a BYE to Bob, and Bob learns of the success, with the dialog identifiers, in a NOTIFY. Carol later retrieves the call by sending Alice an INVITE containing the dialog identifiers, which replaces the session with the Park Server. The RFC notes the same flow could be used for music on hold.

In call pickup, Bob and Bill are in a work group. Alice calls Bob, who does not answer. Bill sends a SUBSCRIBE to Bob to get the dialog information, then sends an INVITE with Replaces to Alice. Alice answers and sends a CANCEL to stop Bob's phone ringing. The early-only parameter on Replaces stops Alice accepting the INVITE if Bob has already answered; omit it to take the call regardless.

In automatic redial, Alice calls Bob, who is busy. Alice subscribes to Bob's call state, Bob sends a NOTIFY when he is available, and Alice's phone alerts her and then sends a new INVITE.

In click to dial, Bob clicks Carol's SIP URI in a web browser. His PC client sends a REFER to his SIP phone, which sets up the session with Carol. The PC uses Refer-Sub: false (RFC 4488) so that no REFER dialog is established. The RFC prefers this to a 3pcc flow because end-to-end signaling is not interrupted by a controller and Bob avoids missing ringback tone or clipped audio.
sections.eli5: Parking a call is like leaving it on a shelf for someone to pick up. Pickup lets a teammate answer your ringing phone. Redial pings you when a busy friend is free, and click to dial lets you start a call by clicking a link.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because many examples involve SIP call control, either peer-to-peer or 3pcc, the security considerations of the Multiparty Framework document apply. Many services also rely on a user agent being part of a group, such as employees in a department, home phone extensions or call center members. Group members get special privileges: a user agent might normally refuse to share detailed dialog information, but share it with a group member to make call pickup possible. Group members must be authenticated using normal SIP means such as certificates or shared secrets.

The examples use REFER, Replaces, Join and the dialog package heavily, so the security considerations of RFC 3515, RFC 3891, RFC 3911 and RFC 4235 apply to these scenarios.
sections.eli5: Some tricks only work if phones trust each other, like coworkers sharing a desk. So the phones must check that someone really belongs to the group before sharing anything.

messages.label: INVITE F1
messages.note: Bob calls Alice; the call is answered and media flows.

messages.label: REFER F5
messages.note: Alice asks Bob to call Carol (Refer-To).

messages.label: BYE F9
messages.note: Alice drops out of the call.

messages.label: NOTIFY F15
messages.note: Reports the success of the transfer.

messages.label: SUBSCRIBE F4
messages.note: Alice subscribes to Bob's call state.
